opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that most of the standard benchmarks out there were designed to answer a fairly narrow question, which is something like: how good is this model at producing a correct or fluent answer on some fixed distribution of tasks? And that's a perfectly reasonable thing to measure, but it's not really the question we care about when we're thinking about deploying these models responsibly in a particular setting.

So, for instance, a lot of my work over the years has been on algorithmic fairness, privacy, and more recently on what you might broadly call responsible AI. And when you come at LLMs from that angle, the existing metrics and datasets have a few limitations that become pretty obvious pretty quickly.

One is that they're mostly aggregate measures. You get a single number, or a handful of numbers, that summarize performance over the whole dataset. But many of the harms we worry about are about disparities: how does the model behave differently for different groups of people, or on different kinds of inputs? An aggregate accuracy figure can look great while hiding the fact that performance is quite poor on some subpopulation. And there's a further subtlety, which I've spent a lot of time on in the classification setting: you don't just care about a few predefined groups like race or gender. You might care about intersections of attributes, or about groups that are defined in more complicated ways, and the number of such groups can be very large. Static benchmarks aren't built to let you audit for that.

A second limitation is that a lot of these datasets have almost certainly leaked into the training data at this point. Once a benchmark has been public for a while and the models are trained on large swaths of the internet, it becomes really hard to know whether you're measuring generalization or memorization. That's a basic statistical problem. In machine learning theory we've always relied on a clean separation between training and test data, and that separation has gotten very blurry.

The third issue is that the use cases themselves are often much more open-ended than the benchmarks. With a classifier, you have a well-defined prediction task and a well-defined notion of error. With a generative model, what counts as a mistake, or a harm, is much more context-dependent. Is this response toxic? Is it biased? Is it a hallucination? Those are often judgment calls, and they depend a lot on the deployment context. A dataset assembled for one purpose may not capture the notion of harm that matters in yours.

So the way I tend to think about it is that existing metrics and datasets are a useful starting point, a kind of sanity check, but if you have a specific use case, you really need to build evaluation that's tailored to it. That means thinking carefully about which behaviors matter, which populations or input types you need to check, and ideally having some ability to generate fresh test cases rather than relying on a fixed static set. And I think there's a lot of interesting science still to be done in making that process more principled, so it's not just ad hoc red teaming but something with real statistical guarantees behind it.

r001.rationale: The response says datasets assembled for one purpose may not capture the harms relevant to a specific deployment, and recommends evaluation tailored to the use case.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth starting with what we actually need these models to do, because that's where the mismatch shows up. The kinds of applications we care about are ones where the model is operating in a regulated, high-stakes setting, where there's a real notion of ground truth, and where getting something wrong isn't just an aesthetic failure, it has consequences. And when you look at the standard benchmarks, the MMLU-style evaluations, the leaderboards, they're really measuring something quite different. They're measuring a kind of broad, general competence on questions that somebody wrote down once, usually with a clean multiple-choice answer.

So the first limitation is just distribution. The data in those benchmarks doesn't look like the data in our use case. Our questions are domain-specific, the vocabulary is specialized, and frankly a lot of the hard cases are the ones where the "right" answer depends on context that isn't in the prompt at all. A model can score very well on a general benchmark and then behave quite poorly on exactly the inputs we care about, and there's no reason the benchmark score would have predicted that.

The second limitation, and this is one I find myself thinking about a lot given my background in learning theory, is contamination. These models have been trained on enormous slices of the internet, and the public benchmarks are on the internet. So you're often not measuring generalization at all, you're measuring something closer to memorization, and you can't easily tell which. That's a problem that's very hard to fix once a data set is public. It essentially has a shelf life.

The third thing is that most of these metrics are averages. They tell you the model gets eighty-some percent right. But for us, the interesting question is almost never the average. It's where are the errors concentrated, are they concentrated on particular subpopulations, particular kinds of inputs, particular individuals, and is the model confident when it's wrong. An aggregate accuracy number just erases all of that structure. And from a fairness and reliability standpoint, that structure is the whole story.

So what we've ended up doing, and I think this is what a lot of serious practitioners are converging on, is treating the public benchmarks as a very coarse screening tool, a way to rule models out rather than a way to rule them in. And then building our own evaluation, with data that actually comes from the deployment distribution, with human judgment in the loop where there isn't a clean label, and with the evaluation designed around the specific failure modes we're worried about. That's more expensive, it's less glamorous, you don't get a number you can put on a leaderboard. But I'd rather have an honest estimate of how the thing behaves in our setting than a flattering estimate of how it behaves in somebody else's.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark data does not resemble the use case, noting that the use case has domain-specific questions and specialized vocabulary, while standard benchmarks use broad, clean questions.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing to recognize is that performance on a general benchmark and performance on your particular application are two different things. A benchmark can be useful for narrowing the set of models you want to consider, but it doesn’t tell you whether a model is going to behave acceptably on the distribution of inputs that your users will actually give it.

And there’s a second issue, which is that the metric itself encodes a choice about what matters. An average accuracy number treats errors in a particular way, whereas in your application, some errors might be much more costly than others. You might care about performance on a relatively rare category of queries, or about whether the model knows when to abstain. Those things can get lost in an aggregate score.

So I would start with the use case: What are you asking the model to do? What would constitute a consequential failure? And then build an evaluation that reflects those questions, using examples that are representative of the application and deliberately testing the failures you’re most concerned about. Existing evaluations are a useful starting point, but they don’t remove the need for that application-specific work.

r001.rationale: The response says general benchmarks may not reflect the inputs users will provide in a particular application and recommends using representative, application-specific examples.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing to recognize is that a benchmark gives you evidence about performance on that benchmark. And there can be a pretty big gap between that and the thing you actually care about in your application. What kinds of questions are users going to ask? What does a mistake look like? And what are the consequences of that mistake?

An aggregate score can hide a lot of variation. A model might do very well on average and still fail systematically on a particular type of task or for a particular group of users. If those failures are consequential in your use case, the average isn't really the right object to focus on.

So I would treat existing evaluations as a starting point. You need evaluations that reflect the actual setting, including the surrounding system and the people using it. And you need to keep checking after deployment, because the distribution of interactions can change. The benchmark is useful evidence, but it isn't a certificate that the system is going to behave the way you want.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark performance can be far from the application’s actual needs and that evaluations should reflect the real setting, communicating that existing evaluation data may not cover the intended use case.
